summary: Defines the DNS SRV record, which specifies where the servers for a given protocol and domain are located, like a more general form of MX. It was experimental, and it was replaced by RFC 2782.

eli5.summary: Besides asking who handles the mail, you can ask who handles any service. SRV records tell where to go.

questions: what is a dns srv record
how to find a service location in dns
what is the difference between priority and weight in srv
subtitle: DNS records for locating services by protocol and domain.

tldr.problem: Before SRV, clients either needed to know a server's exact address or use workarounds like ftp.whatever.com aliases or SMTP-specific MX records. There was no general way to locate services or handle failover.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2052 defines the SRV (Service) DNS record type (type 33), which maps service.protocol.domain to a list of servers with priority and weight fields. Clients query for SRV records to find available servers and select among them based on priority and load-balancing weight.
tldr.outcome: DNS SRV became a standard way to locate services in DNS. This experimental specification was later superseded by RFC 2782, which refined the SRV mechanism.

today: RFC 2052 is an Experimental protocol and has been obsoleted by RFC 2782. The DNS SRV mechanism is now widely deployed for service discovery in modern Internet systems.

sections.title: Service Location in DNS
sections.content:
RFC 2052 solves the problem of locating service servers in the Internet. Without SRV records, clients either had to know the exact address of a server or resort to workarounds like well-known hostnames (ftp.whatever.com) or broadcast queries. The RFC introduces the SRV (Service) record type to provide a general mechanism for administrators to specify which servers handle which services for a domain.

The SRV RR allows administrators to run multiple servers for a single domain, move services between hosts with minimal effort, and designate primary and backup servers. Clients query for a specific service and protocol for a domain and receive back the available servers.
sections.eli5: Instead of hardcoding server addresses, you can ask DNS where to find any service. DNS gives you back a list of servers and tells you which ones are primary and which are backup.

sections.title: The SRV Record Format
sections.content:
The SRV record (DNS type 33) has the format: Service.Proto.Name TTL Class SRV Priority Weight Port Target

The Service field is the symbolic name of the desired service (like http, smtp, telnet), defined in Assigned Numbers or locally. The Proto field specifies the protocol (TCP or UDP). The Name field is the domain being referenced. The Priority field works like MX priority: clients must attempt the lowest-numbered priority first, with higher-numbered servers used as backups (range 0-65535). The Weight field provides load balancing: among servers with the same priority, the probability of selection should be proportional to weight (range 1-65535). The Port field specifies the port number on the target host (0-65535). The Target field is the domain name of the server; a target of '.' means the service is not available at that domain.
sections.eli5: An SRV record says: for service X on protocol Y in domain Z, try these servers in this order, and if they are equally important, spread the load between them based on their weight, and use this port number.

sections.title: How Clients Use SRV Records
sections.content:
SRV-aware clients follow a specific procedure to locate and connect to servers. They query DNS for QNAME=service.protocol.target with QTYPE=SRV. If the reply contains valid SRV records, the client builds a list of (Priority, Weight, Target) tuples and sorts by priority (lowest first). For each priority level, the client selects servers probabilistically using the weight values, building an ordered list. The client then queries for A records for each target host and attempts to connect using the returned addresses and the specified port.

If no SRV records are found, most clients fall back to other mechanisms: for SMTP, they use RFC 974 MX records; for other services, they perform a standard A record lookup on the domain name itself. This backward compatibility allows SRV to coexist with older clients.
sections.eli5: A client asks DNS 'where should I go for the web service?' DNS says 'try server A first at port 80, or server B as a backup at port 8000.' The client tries server A; if that is down, it tries server B.

sections.title: Implementation and Backward Compatibility
sections.content:
Domain administrators should provide both SRV records and fallback A records during the transition period, since most existing clients do not understand SRV. The RFC suggests maintaining lists of reasonable backup hosts at A record level for services likely to be used with the domain name. For services spread across multiple hosts, administrators can provide A records for all hosts (allowing round-robin load balancing) or just the primary host.

The RFC notes that DNS replies are limited to 512 bytes for UDP, so administrators are advised to keep SRV replies below this limit. The memory overhead is roughly 30 bytes for general overhead, 20 bytes per SRV RR plus the target hostname, and similar costs for NS and A RRs in the Additional Data section. A detailed zone file example demonstrates typical SRV usage, including failover scenarios with different priorities and weights.
sections.eli5: Administrators set up both old-style address records and new SRV records so that both old and new software can find the servers. They also need to be careful not to make DNS replies so large they do not fit in a single packet.

sections.title: Security Implications
sections.content:
The RFC discusses security impacts of SRV records. Fine-grained port specification affects packet filtering: routers can no longer simply block external access to specific ports, since the port is now specified by DNS per service. There is also no way for a site to prevent its hosts from being referenced in SRV records, which could lead to denial of service attacks by listing unwilling hosts as servers.

DNS spoofing is somewhat more dangerous with SRV, since attackers can supply false port numbers in addition to false hostnames and addresses. However, the authors note that DNS security extensions (when developed) should return relevant records in the Additional Data section of SRV queries.
sections.eli5: SRV records make it easier for DNS to be spoofed to send you to the wrong server or port. Firewalls also become more complicated because the port is no longer fixed.

fields.name: Weight
fields.desc: Load balancing; selection probability proportional to weight (1-65535).

fields.name: Target
fields.desc: Domain name of target host; '.' means service not available.
